description: How government uses taxation and public spending to manage the economy — budget surplus, deficit and fiscal policy.
content_html:
What Is Fiscal Policy?

Fiscal policy is one of the most powerful tools a government has to manage the economy. Every year, the government collects money through taxes and spends it on public services — schools, hospitals, roads, welfare payments. By changing how much it taxes and how much it spends, the government can boost or slow down economic activity. Think of it as the government turning a dial: spend more and tax less to heat the economy up; spend less and tax more to cool it down.

Government Spending

The government spends on a vast range of areas. The largest items in the UK are social protection (benefits and pensions), the National Health Service, education, and debt interest payments. This spending puts money directly into the economy. When the government builds a new school, construction firms are paid, workers earn wages, and those workers then spend in local shops — the spending ripples outward.

This ripple effect is called the multiplier effect. Each pound the government injects can generate more than a pound of additional economic activity as it circulates through the economy.

Key Fact

Government spending includes transfer payments (benefits, pensions) and spending on public services (health, education, infrastructure). Both inject money into the economy and can increase aggregate demand.

Taxation

The government raises revenue through direct taxes and indirect taxes. Direct taxes include Income Tax (paid on earnings) and Corporation Tax (paid by companies on profits). Indirect taxes include Value Added Tax (VAT), which is added to the price of most goods and services, and duties on fuel and alcohol.

The key difference is who pays: direct taxes are collected from individuals or firms directly; indirect taxes are collected by businesses when consumers spend. Both affect demand in the economy. When the government raises Income Tax, households have less to spend — consumer spending falls, which tends to reduce inflation and growth.

A progressive tax takes a larger share of income from higher earners. In the UK, Income Tax is progressive: people earning above the personal allowance pay 20%, higher earners pay 40%, and the very highest earners pay 45%. This means the rich contribute proportionally more, which can reduce inequality.

A regressive tax hits lower-income earners hardest as a share of their income. Indirect taxes such as VAT are often regressive: a 20% VAT charge on a £100 television takes the same £20 from a low earner and a high earner, but that £20 is a much larger fraction of the low earner’s weekly budget. Fuel duty works the same way — everyone pays the same rate at the petrol pump.

The Government Budget

Each year the government compares its total revenue (mainly taxes) with its total spending. The difference between the two is the budget balance. Three outcomes are possible:

A balanced budget means spending equals revenue — the government is neither borrowing nor saving. A budget surplus means revenue is greater than spending — the government collects more in taxes than it pays out. It can use the extra to pay off existing debt or save for future spending. A budget deficit means spending is greater than revenue — the government is spending more than it collects. To cover the gap it must borrow, adding to the national debt.

Key Fact

Budget balance = Government revenue − Government spending. A surplus means revenue > spending (government can repay debt). A deficit means spending > revenue (government must borrow, increasing national debt).

Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy

Fiscal policy changes deliberately to try to hit government objectives. There are two broad directions:

Expansionary fiscal policy means the government cuts taxes and/or increases spending. This puts more money in households’ and firms’ hands. Demand in the economy rises, which tends to boost output and employment. Governments typically use expansionary policy during a recession — when growth is falling and unemployment is rising — to stimulate activity. The trade-off is that the budget deficit usually widens.

Contractionary fiscal policy means the government raises taxes and/or cuts spending. This takes money out of the economy. Demand falls, which can slow inflation. Governments use contractionary policy when the economy is overheating or when they want to reduce a large deficit. The trade-off is slower growth and potentially higher unemployment.

Students often confuse fiscal and monetary policy. The difference is in the tool used. Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation — it is decided by the government (HM Treasury and the Chancellor). Monetary policy uses interest rates and the money supply — it is set by the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, which has operational independence to decide how to set interest rates. However, the inflation target itself (2% CPI) is set by the government (the Chancellor), not the MPC. Both aim to influence aggregate demand, but through different channels and with different time lags.

An easy memory hook: Fiscal → Finance → government spending & tax. Monetary → Money → interest rates & the Bank of England.

How Fiscal Policy Connects to Government Objectives

The government has four main macroeconomic objectives: economic growth, low unemployment, price stability (low inflation) and a healthy balance of payments. Fiscal policy can help achieve all four, but there are trade-offs.

To boost economic growth: cut taxes or raise spending → aggregate demand rises → firms produce more → GDP grows. To reduce unemployment: increase government spending on infrastructure → construction jobs created directly → multiplier boosts wider employment. To control inflation: raise taxes or cut spending → demand in the economy falls → firms face less pressure to raise prices. The tension is real: the policies that promote growth can also fuel inflation, and vice versa.

Fiscal policy can also address the distribution of income. Progressive income taxes combined with welfare spending redistribute money from higher earners to lower-income households. This can reduce inequality, though critics argue it may reduce incentives to work and invest.

Fiscal policy has significant limitations. First, there are time lags: it can take months or years for a policy change to feed through to the real economy. By the time the effect is felt, the economy may have already turned. Second, large deficits build up national debt, on which the government must pay interest — debt interest payments crowd out spending on schools and hospitals. Third, there is a political dimension: tax cuts are popular, spending cuts are not, so fiscal policy can be distorted by electoral cycles. Finally, expansionary policy may simply lead to higher imports, helping foreign producers rather than UK ones.
exam_tip_html: The command word Evaluate asks you to look at both sides and reach a supported judgement. For a fiscal policy question, do not just list the advantages of cutting taxes — also explain the risks (a wider deficit, higher debt interest, potential inflation). Then decide which argument is stronger and say why. A useful scaffold: “It depends on the state of the economy — if the economy is in recession, expansionary fiscal policy is more likely to raise growth than inflation, but if it is already growing quickly the risk of overheating is greater.” Evaluation marks are won on judgements about conditions, not just listing points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation to manage the economy. Expansionary policy (higher spending, lower taxes) raises demand and growth; contractionary policy (lower spending, higher taxes) reduces demand and can tackle inflation.
  • The budget compares government revenue and spending. A surplus means revenue exceeds spending; a deficit means spending exceeds revenue, requiring borrowing that adds to national debt.
  • Progressive taxes take a higher proportion from higher earners, reducing inequality; regressive taxes (like VAT) take a higher share from lower earners. Fiscal policy trade-offs mean pursuing one objective can make another harder to achieve.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a direct tax?
A) Value Added Tax (VAT)
B) Fuel duty
C) Income Tax
D) Tobacco duty
practice_questions.marks: C) Income Tax [1 mark]. Income Tax is paid directly by the person who earns the income; VAT, fuel duty and tobacco duty are all indirect taxes added to the price of goods.

practice_questions.text: The government collects £850 billion in tax revenue in a year and spends £910 billion. Calculate the budget deficit and state whether this is a surplus or a deficit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: Budget balance = Government revenue − Government spending = £850bn − £910bn; 1 mark for the correct answer of −£60 billion (a budget deficit of £60 billion).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a rise in government spending on infrastructure might reduce unemployment.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the link (government spends more on infrastructure → jobs created in construction); 1 mark for developing the chain (workers earn wages → they spend in shops → more jobs created elsewhere via the multiplier); 1 mark for applying the economic principle (aggregate demand increases, so firms hire more workers to meet higher demand).

practice_questions.text: A government is concerned about rising inflation. Explain how it might use fiscal policy to reduce inflation. Use an example of a named tax or spending measure in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the policy direction (contractionary fiscal policy — raise taxes and/or cut spending); 1 mark for a named measure (e.g. increase Income Tax or reduce welfare spending); 1 mark for the chain of reasoning (households have less disposable income → consumer spending falls → firms face less demand → less pressure to raise prices); 1 mark for the economic conclusion (aggregate demand falls, reducing demand-pull inflation).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a cut in Income Tax might affect the level of economic activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Develops a clear, multi-step chain of reasoning from the tax cut through to at least two economic outcomes (e.g. higher disposable income → increased consumer spending → higher aggregate demand → firms produce more → employment rises; also addresses the multiplier effect or a potential trade-off such as wider deficit or inflationary pressure). Accurately uses economic terminology throughout.

Secure: Explains the direct link between lower Income Tax and higher consumer spending, and connects this to at least one government objective (growth or employment). May miss a second-order effect or the trade-off.

Developing: States that cutting Income Tax increases spending and boosts the economy but the chain is incomplete or only one step is developed.

Emerging: Identifies a link between tax cuts and the economy but with limited development; may lack specific economic terminology.

practice_questions.text:
"Expansionary fiscal policy is always the best way for a government to achieve its economic objectives."
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Expansionary fiscal policy can quickly boost aggregate demand during a recession — higher spending and lower taxes put money into households' and firms' hands, stimulating growth and reducing unemployment.
• Government infrastructure spending can have a strong multiplier effect, creating construction jobs directly and additional jobs through knock-on spending.
• In a period of very low interest rates, fiscal stimulus may be more effective than monetary policy at boosting demand.
• Welfare spending targets those with the highest marginal propensity to consume, maximising the demand boost.

Arguments against:
• Expansionary fiscal policy can cause demand-pull inflation if the economy is already close to full capacity — more money chasing the same output pushes prices up.
• It widens the budget deficit and increases national debt. Higher debt leads to higher interest payments, crowding out future public spending.
• There are significant time lags — by the time the effect is felt the economy may have recovered, making the stimulus counterproductive.
• It may worsen the balance of payments if higher consumer demand sucks in more imports rather than boosting domestic output.
• The aim of "always" the best policy is too absolute — contractionary policy is more appropriate when inflation is the priority rather than growth.

Judgement: The effectiveness of expansionary fiscal policy depends on the state of the economy. It is most appropriate during a recession when there is spare capacity; it is less appropriate when the economy is growing strongly and inflation is already elevated. A supported conclusion should weigh whether the objective targeted (growth vs inflation) aligns with the current economic context.

Mastering: Develops two or more supported arguments on each side, uses economic terminology accurately, and reaches a clear justified judgement that acknowledges conditions under which the statement holds or fails.
Secure: Develops at least one argument on each side with a basic judgement.
Developing: Identifies arguments for or against but only minimally develops them; judgement may be asserted rather than supported.
Emerging: Mostly one-sided or undeveloped; little use of economic concepts.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes fiscal policy?
options: The Bank of England changing interest rates to control inflation
The government using spending and taxation to manage the economy
Firms adjusting their prices in response to changes in demand
The government selling state-owned industries to the private sector

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of tax takes a higher proportion of income from higher earners?
When government spending is greater than tax revenue, the government is running a budget _____.
VAT is an example of an _____ tax, because it is added to the price of goods and paid by the consumer.
Match each fiscal policy term to its correct meaning:
right: Higher spending or lower taxes to boost demand
Higher taxes or lower spending to reduce demand

flashcard_questions.a: The use of government spending and taxation to influence the level of economic activity.
When government spending is greater than tax revenue, requiring the government to borrow.
When government tax revenue is greater than government spending.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a direct tax in the UK.
Give one example of an indirect tax in the UK.
flashcard_questions.a: VAT (added to the price of goods and services at the point of purchase).

flashcard_questions.q: What makes Income Tax a progressive tax?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income in tax.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is VAT considered a regressive tax?
flashcard_questions.a: It takes a higher share of income from lower earners than from higher earners.
Cutting taxes and/or raising government spending to boost aggregate demand.
Raising taxes and/or cutting government spending to reduce aggregate demand.

flashcard_questions.q: A government raises Income Tax during a period of rising inflation. Is this expansionary or contractionary?
flashcard_questions.a: Contractionary — it reduces household spending and cools demand.
An initial injection of government spending leads to a larger overall rise in national income.

flashcard_questions.q: Fiscal policy is controlled by the government. Which independent body controls monetary policy in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee.

flashcard_questions.q: State one trade-off of using expansionary fiscal policy to boost growth.
flashcard_questions.a: It widens the budget deficit and increases national debt.

glossary_terms.definition: The use of government spending and taxation to influence the level of economic activity.
The process by which an initial injection of government spending leads to a larger overall increase in national income.
A tax levied directly on income, profits or wealth, paid by the person or organisation that earns it.
A tax added to the price of goods and services, paid by the consumer when they buy.
A tax that takes a higher proportion of income from those who earn more, making income distribution more equal.
A tax that takes a higher proportion of income from those who earn less, making income distribution less equal.
The annual difference between government revenue and government spending.
